============================================================
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Does U.S. food aid fuel civil conflict?”  
============================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) design using a country-year panel.

Rationale  
•  Endogeneity of food aid: aid is targeted to needy or conflict-ridden places, so OLS will be upwardly biased toward a positive aid–conflict correlation.  
•  Instrument: (U.S. wheat productiont × country i’s long-run aid sharei)  ≡  “shift-share” or “Bartik” shock.  
 –  “Shift” = yearly, plausibly exogenous variation in total U.S. wheat output, driven by U.S. weather and agronomic conditions.  
 –  “Share” = time-invariant propensity of a country to receive U.S. food aid.  
•  The interaction gives country-specific, time-varying predicted aid that is as-good-as-random after flexible country and year fixed effects and controls.  
•  The IV strategy is more credible than DID or event study because the treatment does not start at one moment; it is a continuous flow whose timing/size depends on supply shocks.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Aid_it  = U.S. wheat food aid to country i in year t (metric tons).  
 Alternative scalings: ln(1+aid) or aid per capita.

Control group  
The counterfactual comes from the same set of 125 potential recipients in years when their instrument-predicted aid is low (i.e., we exploit within-country, over-time variation). Country and year fixed effects sweep out permanent differences across countries and common global shocks.

Treatment timing  
Continuous annually, 1971–2006.

No RDD running variable/cutoff is used.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance  
Cov( Z_it , Aid_it ) ≠ 0.  Surplus disposal laws plus historical allocation rules make it highly likely. (Can be tested: F-stat > 10.)

A2. Exclusion (exogeneity)  
Conditional on controls and fixed effects, the interaction Z_it influences conflict only through the quantity of U.S. wheat food aid.  
Plausibility:  
•  U.S. wheat output should not directly affect conflict inside, say, Burundi except through the channel of actual shipments.  
•  Potential violation: global grain prices move with U.S. production and might affect food security/conflict. Will control for FAO world wheat price index × country import dependence.

A3. Monotonicity (shift-share monotonicity)  
For all i, higher Z_it weakly raises expected aid; no country systematically “loses” aid when the instrument rises. Historically plausible because surplus wheat lifts all recipient boats, just in proportion to their fixed share.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-country spillovers)  
Food aid sent to country i does not directly change conflict in country j. May be threatened in contiguous states; will test by dropping neighbors and border countries as robustness.

A5. Correct functional form and linearity  
Assume linear first-stage response; flexible polynomials in time and country FE help.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Instrument affects conflict through world prices, not only through aid.  
Remedy: Control for (U.S. wheat production × country wheat import dependence), FAO world wheat price, and its interaction with import dependence.

T2. Conflict itself changes historical aid shares (endogenous “shares”).  
Remedy: Use shares calculated from the first 10 years (1971-1980) only, or pre-sample colonial era food aid if available, to ensure shares are predetermined.

T3. Serial correlation & clustering bias standard errors.  
Remedy: Cluster at the country level; also two-way cluster by country and year; check robustness with Conley spatial HAC.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ----------------------------------------------
# Packages
# ----------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast feols / feiv
library(sandwich)     # vcov conveniece
library(lmtest)

# ----------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
# ----------------------------------------------
wheat   <- fread("us_wheat_production.csv")          # year, us_wheat_prod
aid     <- fread("usaid_wheat_aid.csv")              # country, year, tons
conflict<- fread("ucdp_prio_conflict.csv")           # country, year, onset, incidence
macro   <- fread("world_dev_indicators.csv")         # gdp_pc, pop, democracy, oil
price   <- fread("world_wheat_price.csv")            # year, price_index

# harmonise country codes
for (df in list(aid, conflict, macro)) df[, iso:=countrycode(country, "country.name", "iso3c")]

# historical aid share (1971-2006, or alternative 1971-80)
hist_share <- aid[,.(hist_share = sum(tons)), by = iso][ , hist_share := hist_share / sum(hist_share)]

# build panel
panel <- merge(aid, conflict, by=c("iso","year"), all=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, macro,   by=c("iso","year"), all=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, wheat,   by="year",          all.x=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, price,   by="year",          all.x=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, hist_share, by="iso", all.x=TRUE)

# ----------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct variables
# ----------------------------------------------
panel[, aid_mt      := fifelse(is.na(tons),0,tons)]
panel[, ln_aid      := log1p(aid_mt)]
panel[, us_wheat_z  := scale(us_wheat_prod)]  # demean & sd-standardise
panel[, instrument  := us_wheat_z * hist_share]

# Outcome(s)
panel[, conflict_any := incidence]     # 1/0
panel[, conflict_onset := onset]       # 1/0

# Controls
panel[, ln_gdppc := log(gdp_pc)]
panel[, ln_pop   := log(pop)]

# Drop missing outcome rows if necessary
reg <- na.omit(panel, cols=c("conflict_any","instrument","ln_gdppc","ln_pop"))

# ----------------------------------------------
# 3. Main IV regression
# ----------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(conflict_any ~ ln_gdppc + ln_pop + democracy + oil_exporter | 
                   iso + year | ln_aid ~ instrument,
                 cluster = ~iso,
                 data = reg)

etable(iv_main, dict = c( "ln_aid"="Food aid (ln+1)",
                          "instrument"="IV: wheat × share"))

# First-stage F-statistic
summary(iv_main, stage = 1)$fs

# ----------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: add world wheat price interaction
# ----------------------------------------------
reg[, import_dep := wheat_imports / (wheat_imports + domestic_prod)]   # if available
reg[, price_int  := price_index * import_dep]

iv_price <- feols(conflict_any ~ ln_gdppc + ln_pop + democracy + oil_exporter + price_int |
                    iso + year | ln_aid ~ instrument,
                  cluster=~iso, data=reg)

etable(list(Main=iv_main, PriceCtrls=iv_price))
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests aid can lower food insecurity (reducing grievances) but also provide a lootable resource and depress farm prices (raising opportunity for rebellion). My prior, consonant with the “resource curse” mechanism, is that exogenous wheat aid marginally increases conflict incidence and onset.  

Magnitude guess: A one-standard-deviation (≈ 100,000 mt) increase in wheat aid raises the probability of conflict incidence by 2–3 percentage points off a baseline of about 12 percent.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1.  Relevance (first-stage F > 10) ................. 1  
C2.  Exclusion (no direct path from Z to Y) ......... 0.5  
C3.  Monotonicity (no defiers) ...................... 0.8  
C4.  No interference across units (SUTVA) ........... 0.7  
C5.  Correct specification / heterogeneous LATE .... 0.6  

Overall: Promising but demands careful robustness and placebo tests.
